    China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It was supposed to be a breakthrough year.
    • In a recent development, much more than diplomatic wording is at stake.
    • A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It was supposed to be a breakthrough year. The Philippines had intended to set up a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea during its 2026 ASEAN presidency. However, at the summit in Manila in mid-November they had to abandon their goal. Some 80% of the text had been negotiated, declared Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, but the key areas of dispute had remained unsolved.

    In a recent development, much more than diplomatic wording is at stake. The South China Sea is one of the world's most vital shipping routes, it is rich in fishing grounds and may harbor significant oil and gas reserves. Primarily, however, it's a region of strategic competition: With its so-called Nine-Dash Line (often drawn in red), China claims a large portion of the sea. Its claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.

    A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating. However, opinions differ, particularly with regard to its binding nature and its geographic scope.

    In a recent development, "The basic problem with establishing such a code of conduct is that China is supremely powerful and has no real interest in a legally binding agreement," remarked political scientist Andreas Ufen, Southeast Asia expert at the German Institute of Global and Area Studies (GIGA). Beijing had little incentive to impose restrictions on itself as long as it was able to pursue its interests in the region even without such an agreement, Ufen told DW.

    The Paracel Islands serve as an example of just how difficult the unresolved issues are. In China, the group of islands is known as Xisha, in Vietnam as Hoang-Sa. Hanoi apparently wants to include them in the code's geographic scope, but China rejects this. An agreement within the ASEAN framework could indirectly affect the territorial claims of the parties involved.

    "A fundamental problem is that so far there's no consensus on whether the code of conduct should be legally binding," said Felix Heiduk, head of research division Asia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). China and the ASEAN nations have been negotiating an agreement for 12 years without major progress so far.

    Recent findings suggest that there were reservations about such a treaty not only in China but also in other ASEAN countries. They would subsequently have to ratify a legally binding agreement under international law in their own countries. A non-binding code of conduct, by contrast, would be little more than a voluntary declaration of intent, Ufen told DW.

    The definition of an "incident" is controversial as well. Are coast guard missions with use of water cannons included? Or blockades of supply vessels? Or is the code only applicable when military force is involved? This will determine which actions will be covered by the regulations in the future.

    According to recent reports, "These are by no means just technical details. Their clarification determines to a great extent whether the code of conduct will in fact be effective or will ultimately remain only a non-binding declaration of intent," Heiduk stated. An agreement without valid commitments would bring about little change.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Ufen views China's attitude as a strategic calculation. "I believe that China is interested in keeping the conflict simmering, so to speak, without having to commit itself to a truly binding legal regulation," he said. In this way, Beijing could strengthen its position in the South China Sea without limiting its room for maneuver.

    At the same time there are also diverging interests within the ASEAN group. The 11 member states are by no means united. The Philippines and Vietnam are particularly vocal in their opposition to China. Malaysia and Indonesia pursue a more restrained approach. Cambodia and Laos have close economic ties with Beijing and don't have any territorial claims in the South China Sea.

    "From the start of the negotiations, the lack of unity within ASEAN has been a problem. In a way, it's a permanent obstacle," Heiduk noted. The group makes decisions based on the consensus principle, which basically means that every member state can block a unified position. Recurring confrontations between China and the Philippines exacerbated the problem by undermining trust and making it more difficult to reach compromises.

    According to recent reports, ufen also believes that diverging interests are a key impediment. "Reconciling them is extremely difficult," he said. China could take advantage of the discord. Beijing preferred bilateral negotiations with individual countries rather than dealing with an entire, united group of nations.

    A study published by the Singapore-based Yusof Ishak Institute (ISEAS)reaches similar conclusions. Not only China but internal divisions within ASEAN stalled negotiations. The authors warn against exclusively relying on a comprehensive, legally binding treaty. Initially, partial agreements  — for example, on crisis communication, rescue operations at sea or maritime environment protection — could be a first step. Developing the 2002 agreement on a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea could also be an intermediate step.

    According to recent reports, ufen doubts whether Beijing is interested in a binding result. "For this reason, I can't really imagine that China has a real interest in a code of conduct that includes legally binding regulations," he said.

    In a recent development, heiduk warns against overestimating the significance of a potential agreement. "Even if the code of conduct was signed at some point, in whichever shape, that would in no way solve the conflict in the South China Sea," he stated. The code could regulate how to handle incidents, but it could not eliminate territorial disputes and competing claims to maritime areas.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    This constitutes the dilemma for ASEAN nations as well, whose foreign policy oscillates between China and US ties: An agreement that's as binding as possible could fail because China and individual member states have reservations. A weak, non-binding code, however, could give the impression everyone agreed but would hardly change conduct at sea.

    The American Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) summed up the situationafter the summit in Manila: "Whatever progress was made this year, it is almost certain that the hardest sticking points remain unresolved.".

    Negotiations will be continued in 2027 under Singapore's chairmanship. Whether this will turn into more than just another diplomatic effort will depend on whether China is prepared to submit itself to regulations which limit its scope of action and whether ASEAN will be able to reach a consensus.

    This article was originally published in German.

    Latest Update: You can reuse your old GoPro in a couple different ways

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Turn your old GoPro can be turned into a dash cam or webcam with little to no effort.
    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
    • Sources indicate that goPros are made to withstand challenging conditions, but one thing they often can't survive is the upgrade cycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Turn your old GoPro can be turned into a dash cam or webcam with little to no effort.

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Sources indicate that goPros are made to withstand challenging conditions, but one thing they often can't survive is the upgrade cycle. As customers upgrade to newer models, their old GoPros often end up forgotten and gathering dust in a drawer. Selling an old GoPro is always an option, but a used action camera with a worn-out battery usually isn't worth much.

    The thing is, even older GoPro models usually have decent specs, so you can repurpose them for other uses. With 1080p or even 4K sensors, they still work great as webcams or dash cams, and in both cases, the battery won't matter much since you can keep it plugged in. If you have a GoPro you no longer use, here are a couple of ways to repurpose it.

    Industry observers note that one of the best ways to reuse an old GoPro is to turn it into a dash cam, especially since it already works much like one. Just attach it to a suction-cup mount on the windshield or dashboard, connect it to a USB port or charger and angle it to capture a wide view of the road ahead. Of course, you'll also want to configure it properly.

    Set the camera resolution to at least 1080p at 30 fps or higher, so you'll have clear footage of everything that happens. Also enable loop recording in the GoPro's settings — you can set recording cycles of 20, 60 or 120 minutes, so that it automatically deletes old footage to make room for new footage. You can also set it to use the maximum storage capacity before overwriting. A good-quality 64GB microSD card is usually enough for hours of 1080p video; just remember to stop recording immediately after an accident, otherwise your GoPro will keep recording until it overwrites everything.

    Similarly, remember to press the shutter button every time you start the car to start recording. If that's too much hassle, there's an experimental feature available through GoPro Labs that makes your GoPro automatically turn on and start recording whenever it receives USB power. This feature, however, is only available for models starting with the Hero 7 Black.

    In a recent development, if you don't need a dashcam, there's another great way to repurpose your old GoPro: use it as a webcam. Many laptops still have poor-quality, low-resolution webcams that struggle in low-light conditions, and a GoPro beats most of them. Depending on the model, your GoPro may already have a built-in webcam mode, too: If you have a GoPro Hero 8 Black or newer, download the GoPro Webcam app on your computer and connect your GoPro via USB. You'll see your GoPro listed as a webcam option in apps like Zoom or FaceTime. Battery life won't be an glitch either, since it will draw power over USB.

    Industry observers note that you can still use older GoPro models as a webcam, but it requires a bit more effort. The Hero 4, 5, 6, and 7 Black have micro-HDMI ports you can use to feed a USB capture device like Elgato's Cam Link 4K, which usually costs around $100. These adapters will make your computer see the GoPro as a webcam, though you'll need a separate power supply if your GoPro's battery has degraded. No matter how you connect your GoPro to your computer, though, mount it on a mini tripod and use a dedicated microphone, as the GoPro's built-in microphones aren't really designed for video conferencing.

    Breaking: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A transcription manufacturer that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.
    • The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage.
    • According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A transcription manufacturer that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

    The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the organization’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

    According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

    The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

    It has been revealed that sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the concern, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

    It has been revealed that sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”.

    Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

    Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, mentioned in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”.

    “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

    The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

    It’s unclear if the organization has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

    Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

    The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

    Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

    “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

    Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the fresh wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

    Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

    In a recent development, “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen stated. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”.

    Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica.
    • So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here!
    • But I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

    So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

    But I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

    Since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re important. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

    Industry observers note that I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an important backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

    It has been revealed that focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s upcoming in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the massive questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

    But I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

    One reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

    Recent findings suggest that the former is important because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

    All of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

    But it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

    It’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

    It has been revealed that we’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

    Sources indicate that I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

    Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week.

    An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

    Levent AlpÃ¶ge mentioned, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

    In a recent development, if found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

    The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months revealed scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

    As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

    It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

    Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

    Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

    AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

    "The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge remarked, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier.".

    "I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

    The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

    Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, mentioned on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

    "I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao stated.

    No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

    According to recent reports, openAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

    More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

    The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

    Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

    A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

    "We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

    A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

    It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

    5 iOS 27.3 changes coming to your Apple devices by 2027

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From new Siri AI tricks to interface tweaks for the iPhone Duo, here’s everything new coming with iOS 27.3.
    • Apple released iOS 27.2 in October, which introduced several improvements to Siri AI, but the company hasn't stopped there.
    • Siri AI arrived with iOS 27 in September and was a huge leap forward for the virtual assistant.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From new Siri AI tricks to interface tweaks for the iPhone Duo, here’s everything new coming with iOS 27.3.

    Apple released iOS 27.2 in October, which introduced several improvements to Siri AI, but the company hasn't stopped there. It has already started working on iOS 27.3, which will be the next major upgrade for iPhone consumers. This upcoming version is still in beta and isn't expected to be released to the public before December, but the first developer preview gives us a good idea of what's coming next for Apple devices. The beta adds even more capabilities to Siri AI, which now integrates better with third-party apps, and also introduces a redesigned Health app. It's also the first version of the OS to enable Siri Recap on the Apple Watch.

    Siri AI arrived with iOS 27 in September and was a huge leap forward for the virtual assistant. October's iOS 27.2 upgrade added support for more languages, such as French, Japanese and Portuguese, and iOS 27.3 will expand Siri AI's capabilities even further. The assistant now has multiple new actions for most of Apple's first-party apps, such as Calendar, Mail, Messages, Photos and Safari. You can ask Siri to create a new playlist for you on Apple Music, schedule an iMessage for later or rotate a photo for you. The update makes Siri much more proactive, and it doesn't stop there.

    Industry observers note that the biggest change in iOS 27.3 is a new API for Siri AI that helps app developers better integrate their apps with the assistant. While some apps can already interact with Siri, these interactions are mostly limited to basic commands and answering questions. Soon, Siri AI will be able to control apps using App Intents, letting you order dinner or book a table just by talking to Siri, for example.

    Apple claims the feature is experimental and intended only for development purposes. Apps with full Siri AI support won't be allowed on the App Store until spring 2027, so you'll have to wait a bit longer to control your favorite apps with Siri. Like the iOS 27.2 update, the upcoming update also adds new languages, namely Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish and Norwegian.

    In a recent development, apple teased a redesigned Health app a while ago with the iOS 27.2 beta but pulled it from the final release. Now, the redesigned Health app is back in the first iOS 27.3 beta, and it looks like Apple is ready to make it available to the public next month.

    The redesign divides the app into three tabs: Insights, Longevity and Browse. With Insights, Apple provides a fresh and easier way to understand your health data, which is especially useful for Apple Watch people. It demonstrates your activity history, average steps, heart rate and sleep data, although it's worth noting that the tab relies on Apple Intelligence, so it only works with iPhone 15 Pro or newer.

    Longevity uses several metrics to give you an overview of your health, letting you know whether everything's in good shape and what to pay closer attention to, such as sleep or hearing. Apple Watch owners will also see a Health Age metric, which compares your numbers to what's typical for someone your age. The app also keeps the Browse tab with all the data available in the Health app.

    Safari in iOS 27.3 gets two new features that users have been asking for for years, starting with Vertical Tabs. Like Chrome and other browsers, Safari users can now switch to a vertical tab layout instead of the traditional top bar. By default, tabs are shown as small icons, but the tab column can also show the page titles. The good news is that the new layout is optional, so if you prefer the classic tabs at the top, you can keep using it.

    The second newly introduced feature is Adaptive Dark Mode, and this is a big one. For years, Safari has supported dark mode on websites, which ensures the page matches the theme you're using on your device. The thing is, many websites never implemented dark mode support, so you were liable to get blinded by a bright white page. Those days are over with iOS 27.3 if you enable Adaptive Dark Mode. When turned on, Safari quickly learns the page's layout and adapts it to dark mode if it doesn't support it natively. It doesn't work on all webpages, but it helps make browsing much more comfortable for those who use dark mode.

    The iPhone Duo is certainly one of the most exciting iPhones of all time, but its new form factor makes it a bit tricky to use one-handed when it's closed. Apple's response to this was to bring Reachability to the Duo with iOS 27.3. Although it shares the same name as the feature introduced with the iPhone 6 in 2014, it now works differently: instead of pulling the screen down, it lets users swipe from the side edges to move the interface to the left or right, closer to their thumbs. It's an accessibility feature that's off by default, but if you don't like using your iPhone Duo folded up, it's definitely worth a try.

    iOS 27.3 brings other improvements to the iPhone Duo, including a revised keyboard with extra padding above the top row of keys, meant to make typing easier on the wide display. Non-Duo owners also get an upgrade, with iOS 27.3 bringing the Duo's upgraded Standby mode to all supported phones. It still requires you to plug your iPhone into a charger and place it horizontally, but at least it now features the same redesigned clocks and widgets available on the Duo.

    It has been revealed that one standout feature of the latest Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 is Audio Intelligence, which turns the Apple Watch into an always-listening AI device . However, Apple shipped the new watches without this feature enabled, promising that it would become available later in 2026. That time is now: the first beta of iOS 27.3 finally enables Audio Intelligence on these models.

    Audio Intelligence consists of two features, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind recaps everything noted in the last 15 seconds. You trigger it by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and the watch demonstrates a transcript of the conversation you just had. The other feature is Siri Recap, which runs silently in the background. During the times and in the locations you set, your Apple Watch will listen to your conversations and summarize key points.

    It has been revealed that to protect your privacy, the feature is opt-in and doesn't transcribe everything that was stated verbatim. It also omits sensitive details such as financial information. The recaps are stored in the Siri app and automatically deleted after a week unless you save them. These features won't be available on older Apple Watch models, so you'll need to buy either a Series 12 or an Ultra 4 to use them once iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3 become available.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet tech giant.
    • Intuit acquired the manufacturer in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
    • Sources indicate that flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the tech giant’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet tech giant. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

    Intuit acquired the manufacturer in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

    Sources indicate that flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the tech giant’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the upcoming cash will be used to repurchase shares.

    Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

    Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game initiative to hold them long term. In just the last year, the tech giant has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

    “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Transparency International notes Queensland’s David Crisafulli was ‘by far the most frequently accessed’ state leader, with 13 meetings.
    • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • Bosses at 10 datacentre companies secured almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers in five states over a three-year period, with experts declaring this is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Transparency International notes Queensland’s David Crisafulli was ‘by far the most frequently accessed’ state leader, with 13 meetings.

    Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

    Bosses at 10 datacentre companies secured almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers in five states over a three-year period, with experts declaring this is “just the tip of the iceberg”.

    Analysis by Transparency International Australia argues these meetings, when combined with political donations, demonstrate “unfettered access” to decision-makers that creates an “uneven playing field”.

    The report found donations from major datacentre companies and their contracted lobbying firms nearly tripled over the past three years from $685,000 to $1.8m, coinciding with increased investment across Australia.

    The analysis found the Queensland leader, David Crisafulli, was “by far the most frequently accessed state premier”, with public diaries showing he has met datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years.

    This included three meetings in as many weeks in August and September with Australia’s largest datacentre operator, NextDC – roughly one month before the organization’s expansion in Melbourne was halted after its power provider delayed construction of new power poles due to community backlash.

    “Those meetings took place shortly before the Queensland premier confirmed a dedicated framework to fast-track datacentre approvals by taking them out of the hands of local councils,” the Transparency International report remarked.

    Crisafulli has embraced datacentre investment and flew to the United States in September to secure a $31.9bn deal with the AI giant Anthropic for what could become Australia’s largest datacentre. His office was contacted for comment.

    In a recent development, during this three-year period, 119 meetings with ministers or premiers were held in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland and the ACT. These are the only jurisdictions to publicly release ministerial diaries. The meetings were mostly held in 2026.

    “These numbers are just the tip of the iceberg.” said Clancy Moore, the chief executive of Transparency International Australia.

    “What we don’t know is how many meetings companies like NextDC, OpenAI and Anthropic and their third-party lobbyists are having with the prime minister and ministers in our federal parliament.

    “Australia’s lobbying laws also don’t cover in-house lobbyists or government relations staff so there’s very little oversight of their activities too.”.

    The report also found Australian manufacturer Firmus Technologies secured 10 meetings with Tasmanian ministers and the premier this year alone. During this period, the company’s expansion in the state has faced sustained backlash from local communities who feel they were not properly consulted.

    The three companies that secured the most meetings with ministers were Amazon Web Services, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC.

    In a recent development, last month, Guardian Australia reported on political donations from Amazon and Macquarie to both major parties, closely aligning with the announcement of multimillion-dollar government contracts or planning developments. Both companies say these donations were not aimed at influencing policy and that their timing was coincidental.

    A shareholder at NextDC’s annual general meeting on Friday said the firm had “a lot of lobbying going on in Canberra” but called on the company to better lobby the public on the benefits of datacentres.

    The organization’s chair, Stephen Flynn, said he was “not sure we are great at lobbying as an industry or as a company” but the world had now changed.

    According to recent reports, “We thought we were just going along and [being] invisible, in the way if you think about all telecommunications systems … [it] is kind of invisible. We just take it for granted. But we can’t do that. We can’t do that as we go forward.”.

    The report has also cited examples of four senior public servants at federal government departments quitting to assume leadership positions at OpenAI, AirTrunk and CDC. Three of these appointments were made this year.

    In September, the president of the Australian Professional Government Relations Association, Sally Mackenzie, mentioned the scale of engagement between industry and ministers was a sign of the system working as intended.

    “What we’re seeing with AI and datacentres is that dynamic playing out at real pace, because the stakes for industry, government and Australians more broadly are so high,” Mackenzie said.

    Recent findings suggest that “Lobbying is an crucial part of the democratic process. It ensures that all stakeholders have the ability to communicate with government.”.

    #58806. Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (568 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.
    • This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.
    • In the newly introduced lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

    This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

    In the newly introduced lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

    The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”.

    Neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings claims that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

    DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”.

    Multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

    Recent findings suggest that the Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

    But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

    As of 2026, DraftKings released “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

    “Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

    In a recent development, “Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”.

    In June 2026, DraftKings launched what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”.

    Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

    Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

    “Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”.

    #58804. How to cancel your Nintendo Switch Online subscription

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How to cancel your Nintendo Switch Online subscription

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You’ll have to switch off auto-renewal to cancel, and it’s pretty easy to do so.
    • Nintendo Switch Online gives you access to features that could make gaming more enjoyable, like playing online with friends even if they're halfway around the world, for supported games like Mario Kart World and Animal Crossing: Upcoming Horizons.
    • According to recent reports, but what if, upon looking at it closely, you've decided that paying for Switch Online is no longer worth it?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You’ll have to switch off auto-renewal to cancel, and it’s pretty easy to do so.

    Nintendo Switch Online gives you access to features that could make gaming more enjoyable, like playing online with friends even if they're halfway around the world, for supported games like Mario Kart World and Animal Crossing: Upcoming Horizons. The service also lets you play retro games originally released for Nintendo's old consoles, including the Game Boy and the NES, on your Switch. If you have a Switch 2 and pay for the service's Expansion Pack, you can even play games made for the GameCube. In addition, it gives you access to exclusive games and cloud save, and you'll be able to talk to your friends via a feature called GameChat on the Switch 2.

    According to recent reports, but what if, upon looking at it closely, you've decided that paying for Switch Online is no longer worth it? Maybe you don't use its features as much and won't miss them if you stop paying for the service. Maybe you're cutting down on subscriptions, and Switch Online has to go.

    According to recent reports, the good news is that canceling your membership is fairly easy. Just take note that you can't get a refund for unused days if you cancel in the middle of your subscription term. For example, if you paid $20 for a full year, you can't get $10 back because you canceled six months in.

    For Nintendo Switch Online, you have to switch off auto-renewal, which is supposed to kick in by the end of your current membership period, to cancel a subscription. When you switch off auto-renewal, you can prevent Nintendo from charging your payment method when your current term expires. One important thing to note, however, is that you must turn off auto-renewal at least 48 hours before your membership is set to end. If you're unsure about keeping your subscription, we suggest switching it off early on. You won't be losing access the service's features anyway and can still enjoy its benefits, as long as the subscription term you've already paid for hasn't ended yet.

    You can change your auto-renewal settings on a computer or your Switch console. On a Switch, go to the eShop, select the account that pays for the membership plan and then click on the icon on the upper-right corner to access its Account Information. Click the Nintendo Switch Online section on the left menu and then the Cancel Your Subscription by Turning Off Automatic Renewal button. On a Switch 2, you'll find the Cancel Your Subscription by Turning Off Automatic Renewal option within your Account Information page. Clicking the button will show you a notice that indicates you can still continue using the service until your pass expires at a certain date.

    On a phone or a computer, go to the Nintendo accounts portal and sign into the account that purchased the membership plan. Select Nintendo Switch Online and then find Cancel Your Pass by Turning Off Auto-Renewal in the Active Plan section. Choose Confirm. While you're in there, you may want to change your log-in method too: Nintendo is ending Google and Apple account sign-ins in early 2027.

    It has been revealed that if you have a family subscription, auto-renewal will be turned off for all members of the group. Take note that once your turn auto-renewal off, you can't turn it on again. If you want to continue your membership after all, you'll just have to purchase a new subscription pass for the service.

    Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.
    • But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
    • Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.

    But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.

    Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.

    Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.

    Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.

    And on Sunday morning, German media including tabloid BILD and broadcaster Sport1 reported that Musiala had suffered another seizure as recently as last Monday, believed to be a result of an adjustment to his medication.

    Musiala was deemed fit to feature against Cologne on Friday but the most recent incident prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.

    "It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.

    "It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances.".

    Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable.".

    Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge noted he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his newly introduced contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.

    "I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem.".

    Rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma.".

    "He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," said Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money.".

    Recent findings suggest that bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks.".

    The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.

    The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better.".

    Industry observers note that "Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise.".

    Sources indicate that former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala.".

    The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.

    One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and noted that patients suffering from such conditions require "support.".

    He mentioned Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.

    Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern.".

    Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.

    In a recent development, "When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," noted Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club.".

    Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.

    "We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've noted that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the fresh year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract.".

    President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a new contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.

    "I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.

    But the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker stated it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.

    "He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure.".

    German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form.".

    In a recent development, meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the fresh year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.

    And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
    • Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
    • The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

    Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

    The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

    Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

    Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

    The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

    In a recent development, the speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

    Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

    Recent findings suggest that despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

    The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

    Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the firm was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

    Recent findings suggest that some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI firm experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

    Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

    While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

    "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

    "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability.".

    Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

    Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the firm was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

    In a recent development, musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it declared a bond sale to finance what the tech giant said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

    But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

    Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

    Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

    Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

    Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

    South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

    Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (664 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
    • The data center ecosystem at the moment depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
    • Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

    The data center ecosystem at the moment depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

    Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

    But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

    That may not matter to the manufacturer in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

    In a recent development, however, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

    Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

    Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

    That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

    Breaking: You can mass-delete all of your emails on Gmail in only a few clicks

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you have thousands of emails piling up in Gmail, this is for you.
    • You're more than welcome to delete your emails individually if you want to be there for a very long time.
    • In your computer browser (mobile browsers didn't make the cut), click on the Gear icon in the upper right corner to open Settings > See All Settings > Conversation View.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you have thousands of emails piling up in Gmail, this is for you.

    You're more than welcome to delete your emails individually if you want to be there for a very long time. At two seconds per email, it would take a little over 11 hours of constant clicking to get through 20,000 emails — and honestly, 20,000 emails isn't much for a business Gmail account. Most people are familiar with methodically deleting 50 or even 100 emails at a time by checking the box in the top left and hitting the trash icon. But if you just want to wipe clean your entire inbox and start from scratch, you can do so on a browser.

    In your computer browser (mobile browsers didn't make the cut), click on the Gear icon in the upper right corner to open Settings > See All Settings > Conversation View. Scroll down and tap Conversation View On. Now, go to your inbox. Check the box at the top of the message list to select all the current emails on the page. Once you check the box, a narrow banner should pop up at the top that gives you the option to select all (number of emails) conversations in Primary. Choose that option, take a deep breath, click the trash icon and confirm. Jump over to your Bin in the left column, select it and choose Empty Bin Now > Confirm.

    Industry observers note that if there's a particular thread you're concerned about, enter the name of the business, entity or person you want to find in the Ask Gmail search box at the top. The page will generate all conversations that have anything to do with the term you entered. Right-click one of those emails, select Find Emails From (insert search term), and skim the resulting page, archiving or otherwise protecting those emails from deletion.

    There are a few tabs at the top of a default Gmail inbox, potentially with more categories depending on whether you've added some in the past. One of these tabs is labeled "Promotions," and these emails are probably the most aggravating besides Spam. Fortunately, you can mass-delete them in the same way. Click on Promotions > check the box at the top-left > Select all (number of Promotions emails) conversations in Promotions > Trash Icon > Confirm. You can rinse and repeat with every tab you want to wipe out.

    If you want to be a little more specific, you can also search. Type (category: promotions older_than: 1y) into the search bar to target all Promotions emails that are more than a year old. You can narrow it further by clicking on Showing most relevant and switching it to Showing most recent in the drop-down. Either way, Gmail's tools are fairly extensive, so you don't have to mass-delete every email in every tab, especially if you're worried about deleting something important. Once it's gone from the bin, it's gone for good.

    Sources indicate that archive first and delete later. Archiving removes mail from your inbox, but the messages remain in All Mail and are searchable for future reference. Use the same select-all process; only click Archive instead of the trash icon. In the search bar, specify the emails you want to keep. For instance, type is: starred, is: key or has: attachment. Toss some keywords in there if you're afraid of losing something more specific within those categories, like "offer" or "invoice." Using terms like "from: (email address)" will narrow it down to a specific email sender that you want to delete or keep.

    It's never a bad idea to at least skim through before you mass-delete everything you've received in your inbox over the last year or two. Using search terms makes it much easier, but it'll leave you a little cross-eyed if you stare at the screen long enough. Your best bet is to leave everything in the trash bin for a few days, just in case you remember an important sender and you need to move it back to your inbox.

    #58796. Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1996 w)
