    US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
    • Recent findings suggest that the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
    • Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

    Recent findings suggest that the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

    Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

    Problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

    That caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

    An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a new router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

    According to recent reports, specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a fresh Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

    FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union mentioned that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

    According to recent reports, similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

    To get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

    (This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

    Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

    Sources indicate that philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

    According to recent reports, as an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

    To kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

    It has been revealed that and then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

    In a recent development, so you blueprint around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

    According to recent reports, and even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

    That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

    Sources indicate that it even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

    And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

    L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a massive network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

    (Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

    I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

    Sources indicate that so there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

    In a recent development, now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

    Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

    Recent findings suggest that mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and says, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification?     So, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

    Maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a new hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

    But this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

    Industry observers note that it’s crucial to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

    Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

    Mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has stated that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

    Sources indicate that ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

    It has been revealed that mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

    Sources indicate that but they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

    But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

    According to recent reports, it is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

    Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

    I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

    Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

    It has been revealed that mann: An important caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

    It has been revealed that but what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not said it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

    Sources indicate that one of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

    So in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

    According to recent reports, do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that indicates a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

    It has been revealed that so it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the latest router significantly change anything?     Then, and this is the important part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

    According to recent reports, that may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

    Sources indicate that it is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

    In a recent development, you’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

    In this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

    Ars Technica: The router installation problem that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

    Industry observers note that mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there.     In a recent development, ars Technica: Many people have noted the coincidence of the FAA’s SMART AI system being deployed nationwide in the same week as the router issue that led to the ground stop. The FAA has stated the SMART rollout had no connection to what ensued. What is your view on all this?

    According to recent reports, mann: I get that. I think it is a coincidence. This particular router was just one of a long series of these replacements being done—they don’t take 1,000 routers and just replace them all on a Thursday. They might do one or two of them a night for a couple of years.

    Now, just to lean into it a little bit, it could be totally possible that the router’s capabilities, or maybe something that was configured or misconfigured, is a facilitating technology for SMART. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

    If you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

    But you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

    According to recent reports, but the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

    To the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

    SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

    That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and notes, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

    #58776. What the little clock icon at the top of your Samsung phone means

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (757 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    What the little clock icon at the top of your Samsung phone means

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Three different icons can pass for a clock on your Galaxy phone, and each one has an easy fix.
    • You're fiddling on your phone and that bar at the top of your screen is peppered with various icons.
    • There are tons of icons that can show up in your Android status bar, so what exactly does that clock represent?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Three different icons can pass for a clock on your Galaxy phone, and each one has an easy fix.

    You're fiddling on your phone and that bar at the top of your screen is peppered with various icons. There's your battery level, the Wi-Fi icon, the signal bars — but what's that tiny clock doing there?

    There are tons of icons that can show up in your Android status bar, so what exactly does that clock represent? Is there something wrong with your phone? Well, the good news is that it's rarely a cause for concern, unless you're terrified of waking up bright and early (which we get). Depending on the exact shape, the clock icon usually points to one of a few straightforward explanations, each with an easy fix. There's a good chance that the icon indicates you have an active alarm set up.

    Let's dive deeper into what the clock icon means, how to get rid of it and which other symbols might be causing similar confusion on your Galaxy device.

    The most likely reason you're seeing a clock icon on your screen is that you set an alarm on your phone. Specifically, you've done this through Samsung's Clock app and not some other tool. You'll find the clock right next to the Wi-Fi signal when the entire Quick Settings panel is expanded.

    When the alarm is 30, 15 or five minutes away from ringing, as per the clock settings, the clock icon becomes visible whenever you check your phone, moving to the left of the screen next to the time. In my testing, however, it also popped up at the 20- and 10-minute markers. When you swipe down the notifications panel, you'll even notice a message asking if you want to turn off the upcoming alarm. If you dismiss the notification, the clock icon only remains visible next to the Wi-Fi signal, going back to the original view. The icon shows up again as the alarm time approaches.

    Sources indicate that the only way to make the clock icon go away completely is to disable any active alarms. You'll have to go to the Clock app on your Samsung phone, tap the Alarm tab at the bottom and toggle off or delete any alarms you have set up. Once that's done, the icon immediately vanishes from the status bar.

    It has been revealed that not every clock-shaped icon is an alarm you forgot you set up, however. If you see a rounded square with a small clock inside, it means your phone has a upcoming software patch available. You've probably had your phone pester you about that update and you've ignored it time and time again, so now it's a simple symbol in your status bar. The only way to dismiss this one once and for all is to actually install that update — sorry to break it to you, but you'll have to let the phone do its thing for a few minutes.

    Go to Settings and scroll down to Software update. Select Check for updates to install the latest version of One UI. One UI 9 is currently rolling out to more and more Samsung Galaxy phones, so you're likely due for that update anyway. For some older phones, One UI 9 is the final major update.

    These two are not the only clock-looking symbols you can find in the bar on a Samsung phone. There's another one that gets mistaken for a clock: the Light performance profile indicator. This one is found exclusively on newer Samsung flagship models, such as the Galaxy Z Flip 4 and later, Galaxy Z Fold 4 and later, and Galaxy S23 and later models. This icon looks more like a speedometer than a clock and also features a small white leaf.

    The Light performance mode is designed to reduce power consumption. It will do this by lowering the phone's processing speed, which in turn helps extend battery life. It's a great tool to use when you're scrolling through social media or watching videos. If you start a game, the mode is automatically disabled so you can enjoy all that your phone can actually do.

    If you don't know how the Light performance mode got turned on, you probably touched the icon in the Quick Settings panel by mistake. Just swipe down from the top of the screen and look for the tile and tap it again. Whatever icon you were looking at, you should now know how to get rid of it.

    AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that it’s a significant week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab.
    • “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
    • The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that it’s a significant week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most key problems in mathematics.

    “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

    The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

    Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this ….

    The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

    For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

    But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

    It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

    Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

    Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”.

    However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

    Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another vital proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

    Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

    Sources indicate that in a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”.

    This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.

    Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels.

    A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

    The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a latest youth mobility scheme.

    However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

    Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband noted "all the options will be on the table".

    It came after the prime minister noted that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

    What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

    Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more.

    Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow.

    UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

    The prime minister mentioned the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.

    EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

    Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

    In a recent development, "President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She remarked there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

    Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely.".

    "The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely.".

    Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no latest contributions to the EU budget.

    He said previously declared agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

    Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

    Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

    He mentioned that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

    "Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

    Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch mentioned the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

    She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and remarked the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

    Reform UK leader Nigel Farage stated Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

    Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud.".

    Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey noted there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

    It has been revealed that "A youth mobility scheme is a massive step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole upcoming deal that actually works for Britain, and fast.".

    Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison stated closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the concern of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

    He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

    He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway.".

    Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle noted the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.

    She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals.".

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.
    • China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
    • According to recent reports, wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, remarked: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.

    China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

    According to recent reports, wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, remarked: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”.

    China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

    But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

    According to recent reports, in an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”.

    Experts have noted electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

    While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national intends.

    Recent findings suggest that but campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

    Industry observers note that last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

    Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

    Recent findings suggest that china still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some upcoming ones, though fewer than before. Wang stated this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

    According to recent reports, one of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

    In a recent development, wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”.

    Sources indicate that china is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

    Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU stated it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

    Sources indicate that wang called for more work on trade challenges at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he mentioned. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”.

    Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, remarked other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”.

    Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a latest draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

    • In a recent development, “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve stated it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

    In a recent development, “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”.

    Industry observers note that if Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

    It has been revealed that for the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad mentioned.

    It has been revealed that while Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the organization was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

    In a recent development, for now, at least, Valve indicates it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

    Valve notes it looks to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

    #58768. 5 Apple Watch settings that can help you save its battery life

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1406 w)
    📖 Baca
    EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Apple Watch settings that can help you save its battery life

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A few changes can help give your Apple Watch extra hours of battery when you need it all day.
    • Among the improvements the Apple Watch receives with each iteration, battery life is something everyone wants more of.
    • It has been revealed that if your Apple Watch's battery health has depleted significantly, bringing it in for a battery replacement could help restore its original endurance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A few changes can help give your Apple Watch extra hours of battery when you need it all day.

    Among the improvements the Apple Watch receives with each iteration, battery life is something everyone wants more of. The manufacturer touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 lasts for 24 hours on a full charge. Apple measures this using a combination of 300 time checks, 15 minutes of app use, six hours of sleep tracking, 90 notifications and a 60-minute workout alongside music playback. Real-world results will naturally vary depending on how much you use your Apple Watch every day.

    It has been revealed that if your Apple Watch's battery health has depleted significantly, bringing it in for a battery replacement could help restore its original endurance. You can check battery health status on your watch by navigating to Settings > Battery > Battery Health. Power users might want to look at the Apple Watch Ultra 4 as their next buy since it's better equipped to handle constant, demanding usage with its larger battery.

    Industry observers note that that mentioned, there are a handful of software tricks you can use to squeeze more battery life out of your existing Apple Watch, especially if it's not yet due for a battery replacement. Some of these are simple toggles to enable, while others involve making small adjustments to how you use your watch throughout the day.

    The easiest way to extend your Apple Watch's battery life when it's running low is to turn on Low Power Mode. You can access this feature by pressing the side button, tapping the battery percentage and selecting Low Power Mode.

    Recent findings suggest that an information card will display the first time you use this feature — scroll down and tap on Turn On. Alternatively, you can choose to keep Low Power Mode on for one, two or three days if you know you'll be away from a charger for a while. You can also access this battery saver feature by heading to Settings > Battery.

    A few changes are immediately noticeable when you turn Low Power Mode on. The Always On display is disabled, as are the Wrist Flick and Double Tap gestures. Your watch will still light up its display automatically when you raise your wrist. Background heart rate and blood oxygen measurements are also paused; you can use their respective apps to get manual readings at any time, but low, high or irregular heart rate notifications are disabled. Losing basic health tracking features can be a dealbreaker to many.

    Recent findings suggest that apple says that Siri requests can take longer on the Apple Watch when it's in Low Power Mode, too. Live Activities and the complications on your watch face will update less frequently and scrolling may stutter a bit. Your Apple Watch will continue to receive notifications and calls, but only if its paired iPhone is nearby. When you launch an app that requires internet access, Low Power Mode temporarily turns on Wi-Fi or cellular data.

    The Apple Watch works best when it's near its paired iPhone, but it can also connect to the internet on its own when needed. Any Apple Watch can connect to Wi-Fi networks, while cellular models offer even greater freedom by utilizing mobile data.

    However, Apple recommends keeping the two devices nearby when you need to maximize battery life on your watch. This is because the Apple Watch piggybacks on its paired iPhone's internet connection over Bluetooth. When your devices are connected, you'll spot a tiny green phone icon in Control Center on your Apple Watch.

    Cellular connectivity is convenient, but if you're somewhere that has Wi-Fi available, using that instead can conserve battery life. When you're not actively using your watch and don't mind it being disconnected for a while, you can stretch its endurance even further by enabling Airplane Mode. Find all these toggles in Control Center or access them through the Settings app.

    Industry observers note that even without access to an internet connection, your Apple Watch can track workouts, play music or podcasts that have been downloaded, make purchases using Apple Pay and track your sleep. A good chunk of the built-in apps, like Alarms, Timers, Medications and Voice Memos, also work just fine.

    Sources indicate that the Apple Watch is much more than just a fitness tracker. It can come in handy when your iPhone isn't nearby and you receive a call or message. Newer models come with improved speakers capable of playing music directly. And when you install an app on your iPhone, your Apple Watch will automatically install its companion version (if available).

    This is all great for convenience, but means your watch might end up with a bunch of apps you don't really need on your wrist. Those apps might also increase battery consumption by refreshing in the background and sending you notifications. Using the built-in speakers consumes more battery than connecting headphones does.

    Industry observers note that start by uninstalling unneeded apps from your watch directly, which doesn't remove them from your iPhone. If you use an app on your Apple Watch occasionally but don't need it constantly fetching new information, navigate to Settings > General > Background App Refresh and turn its toggle off. It's also an option to disable Background App Refresh entirely, but this will affect all apps on your watch.

    In a recent development, you can also disable certain app notifications if you don't want your watch constantly buzzing on your wrist. By default, app notifications you've disabled on your iPhone will also be disabled on your Apple Watch, but you can customize which apps send notifications to your watch independently through the Watch app on your iPhone.

    Navigate to Notifications, scroll down to the Mirror iPhone Alerts From section and disable the toggles for any apps you don't want sending notifications to your Apple Watch. Fewer notifications mean fewer vibrations, fewer screen wake-ups and thus potentially less battery drain throughout the day.

    For a more granular approach, you're able to turn off Always On display without giving up the other features Low Power Mode shuts off. On your Apple Watch, navigate to Settings > Display & Brightness > Always On and turn the toggle off.

    Sources indicate that alternatively, this menu has options to customize what information indicates on the Always On display, such as Live Activities or complication data. Macworld tested how significant of a difference turning this feature off makes, and reported that disabling Always On display extended battery life on the Apple Watch by an impressive 10 to 12 hours.

    To minimize screen-on time, always cover your watch with your palm when you're done using it. You might also want to turn off the Wake on Wrist Raise toggle (in the same menu) to prevent your watch from lighting up accidentally. Since Low Power Mode disables other gestures, it's fair to assume that shutting off features like Double Tap and Wrist Flick could help conserve a little more battery. You can find these toggles by navigating to Settings > Gestures.

    If you don't like the barebones feel of the Apple Watch when using Low Power Mode, you can configure it to only kick in during specific workouts. This is a great option if you regularly track longer exercise sessions and are willing to sacrifice some workout tracking features in exchange for longer battery life. In watchOS 27, the Workout app introduced two new options that turn Low Power Mode on during workouts.

    It has been revealed that open the Workout app, select an activity type and tap the Goals and Targets button in the top-right corner. Scroll down and tap on Extended, then select Extended Workout to start tracking your activity. Some workouts have a second Max Extended Workout option as well that reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate measurements. It will also disable alerts, splits and certain metrics like current pace during the workout. Once you finish the exercise, Low Power Mode will automatically turn off.

    Industry observers note that if you want the battery saver feature to kick in automatically every time you start a workout, navigate to Settings > Workout and turn the Low Power Mode toggle on. This eliminates the need for you to manually select the Extended Workout option each time — it's one of those underrated Apple Watch features that are easy to miss.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
    • Industry observers note that the U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer.
    • According to recent reports, nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

    Industry observers note that the U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

    According to recent reports, nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

    According to recent reports, pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in Fresh Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

    Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

    Industry observers note that like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

    Sources indicate that fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

    Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

    “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

    COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.
    • After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.
    • "We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

    After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

    "We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," mentioned Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

    He noted adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required.".

    Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

    Recent findings suggest that "Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation remarked.

    The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠noted the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

    Recent findings suggest that pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," noted the Pakistan negotiator.

    According to recent reports, the marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing. Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

    "You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

    The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs.".

    Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

    Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed looks for a global transformation.".

    At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

    It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

    According to recent reports, the talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot.".

    The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”.

    It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

    In a recent development, scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

    Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu remarked carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve.".

    Industry observers note that the stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

    At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

    Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, remarked his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

    It has been revealed that "We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation.".

    With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

    • Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025.
    • A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
    • Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025.

    A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

    Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.

    The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.

    Sources indicate that rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.

    Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year.

    Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

    One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

    "We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," stated Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

    Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

    Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

    Lawyers for the defendant stated they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

    Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

    "So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality.".

    Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

    They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that highlighted his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

    They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

    The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

    • Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones.

    A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official notes.

    Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.

    Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.

    The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.

    “All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.

    Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.

    Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.

    “When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the tech giant’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he mentioned.

    The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

    The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.

    Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.

    In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police remarked.

    In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.
