    #58648. Industry News: Why data centers are at the center of the Massive Tech backlash

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3775 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why data centers are at the center of the Massive Tech backlash

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
    • Sources indicate that the book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections.
    • Recent findings suggest that in an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.

    Sources indicate that the book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.

    Recent findings suggest that in an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”.

    It has been revealed that “It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”.

    He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”.

    During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.

    I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?

    Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.

    I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.

    According to recent reports, obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these massive fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.

    Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.

    It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.

    According to recent reports, before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s crucial, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?

    In a recent development, I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.

    Industry observers note that and then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.

    Sources indicate that and then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first tech giant-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.

    Recent findings suggest that that was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.

    Recent findings suggest that you don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.

    In a recent development, absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.

    They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.

    I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies, but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.

    And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT.

    Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying glitch?

    Recent findings suggest that because it’s not an abstract matter, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world.

    But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water,. potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.

    In a recent development, I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with.

    Obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.

    There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? It doesn’t often seem like very much.

    The tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and  OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that they’re not going to use NDAs anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make?

    Recent findings suggest that I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition.

    Sources indicate that we’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity.

    Recent findings suggest that when we look at the NDAs and the decision or the announcement that they’re not going to use those anymore, I think it’s also because it’s working against them. People know what a data center is now, and if people find out that a data center is coming to town and they have questions and they’re not getting answers, that’s only going to further fuel the opposition to those data centers.

    Recent findings suggest that so, it’s not really a surprise to see [the tech companies] do this, and it’s a way that they can get a positive PR thing by saying, “We’re not going to use these NDAs that are working against us anyway. “.

    In a recent development, one of the other ways they’ve responded is by saying that there’s a lot of misinformation about the environmental harms, or that they’re being overstated, or that they can mitigate them with renewable technology. How valid do you think those arguments are?

    I think that the industry recognizes that there is a lot of concern and they’re trying to basically move into the discussion with narratives of their own to have people question whether data centers are really a problem or not.

    It has been revealed that I feel like we don’t see the industry doing as much on the energy side anymore, particularly on the fossil fuel side, because they realize that they have kind of lost that argument. If you look back a year and a half, two years ago, they were talking a lot about renewables, about nuclear energy, you don’t hear so much of that discourse anymore.

    According to recent reports, they have pivoted, instead, to focus on the water question, where I think that they feel that they can use more abstract national figures in order to confuse the public about what’s going on. They can say, “If you look nationally, agriculture and golf courses also use a lot of water. So you don’t need to be worried about a data center coming to tow,n because they don’t use as much, in aggregate.”.

    But the matter with data center water use is not a national issue. It’s a local issue. There are unquestionably going to be communities where they seek to locate data centers that are going to have plenty of water and that are not going to be concerned about a data center coming to town. But they’re also locating [data centers] in a lot of communities that are experiencing high degrees of water stress, which means that they don’t have the water to really provide to these infrastructures.

    We have also seen them pivoting to move away from the evaporative cooling systems, the ones that require a lot of water — because you need to take in a certain amount of water as it gets too hot, it evaporates away, and so you can see why you need a consistent flow of water into the data center for that type of cooling system —  to a closed loop system, where you basically have a certain amount of water, it stays within the data center, you keep cooling it down by using electricity to do that, and so you clearly don’t need as much water.

    Industry observers note that that is their newly introduced way to say, “Hey, don’t worry about the water use. We’re going to switch to this other system.” But the issue there, of course, is that it does require more electricity in order to keep that water cooled down, and that is often not part of what they talk about or discuss when they are proposing that as an alternative.

    Then the other thing is that it’s not just water that is in those pipes or tubes going through the data center. There’s also a lot of coolant in there, a lot of chemicals, and communities where these projects are being located with closed loop cooling systems are becoming increasingly concerned about those coolants leaking out into their water supply and what that is going to mean.

    Sources indicate that in the book, you say repeatedly that you’re not against technology itself or even data centers in general, but [against] this hyperscale approach. The book is called “Hyperscale.” The last chapter is called “Human Scale.” Why do you see scale as such an important part of the problem?

    Because scale is what creates the pressures, whether those are the pressures on the communities or you know the pressures on our wider electricity system and whatnot.

    Sources indicate that I don’t think that the inherent problem is data centers, because we have had data centers for a long time, and sure, there have been occasional concerns about specific projects, but data centers as a whole have not been an issue that the public has felt merited this degree of attention. So that is why I feel the hyperscale data center, and particularly the acceleration that we’ve seen in the expansion of the size of these hyperscale data centers, but also the number of data centers that these companies are building out, is notable in this moment.

    In a recent development, linked to that is not just the scale of the demand created by these hyperscale data centers, but also, what they are supposed to be powering? That is where the other disconnect lies. They’re demanding a lot, but if we were actually getting something good for it, this might be justified. I think that for a lot of people, and I feel like we see this reflected in polling, they’re not actually seeing the benefits from generative AI.

    In a recent development, so then the question becomes: “Okay, we’re expending all of these resources, we’re pushing up emissions such that climate change is going to be accelerated just to build out all these data centers to meet the ambitions of generative AI that the tech companies have, but then we’re not actually getting much benefit out of that technology. So what are we actually doing here?”.

    Sources indicate that one other thing that really struck a chord with me was your description about how tech executives often talk about the future as if there’s [just one] inevitable future. The only thing that’s in question is how promptly we arrive there [and] who’s going to make the most money off of it.

    This is so crucial for me, because I do feel like how we think about the future then shapes decisions that we make. The tech billionaires, they see the future in a certain way […] and I think that they have been very successful in getting us to buy into their vision of the future for the past several decades. But that does not mean that that is the only way that the future has to be.

    We can imagine a very different kind of future, and that would mean that we place our resources in different places and actually develop technology in a different way, toward different outcomes, with different incentives driving that work.

    Recent findings suggest that there are interesting conversations happening in different parts of the world right now around things like digital sovereignty, getting off of these technologies from the U.S. tech companies. But in some cases, those conversations are promptly captured by industry in those different parts of the world to say, “Okay, we want to get off U.S. technology, but let’s have our local companies do effectively the same thing, and just let them do the same exploitative practices and make the money that the U.S. tech companies would be making.” And I don’t think that that is the right way forward.

    It has been revealed that I also think that there is a role for public sector development of technology in a way that we’ve eschewed or even looked at skeptically for the past number of decades, because the idea was that technology had to be left to the private sector. What we’re starting to see in Europe is a bit more funding of public technology, in order to develop the services that government itself depends on, and I think that that is a good first step.

    But especially when we’re looking at the Microsoft outage that happened just recently, and we’re looking at Google threatening schools with their access to Google search if they don’t accept Google AI tool, I think that there’s a real moment right now to put resources into developing something different, that doesn’t come from these major tech companies, and that hopefully can have much more public benefit than what these companies now provide us.

    COP31 fails to reach major climate deal as talks expose deep divisions

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Countries have failed to reach a major upcoming deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
    • Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
    • But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Countries have failed to reach a major upcoming deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

    Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

    But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

    Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

    The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

    UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, remarked he was "deeply disappointed".

    He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

    After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

    Sources indicate that but the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

    The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

    "It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he noted.

    Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

    A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

    Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

    Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too rapidly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

    Whatâs next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

    Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.

    Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.

    According to recent reports, but this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

    "Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.

    The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

    "This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she noted, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".

    While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

    Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

    Industry observers note that he pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he noted, raising the stakes.

    The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

    And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

    In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

    The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

    Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

    But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

    Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

    Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

    The COP31 president also mentioned that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035.

    But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

    The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, noted he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

    "[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.

    Sources indicate that the UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia.

    A suspected Ukrainian drone attack caused an explosion on a Russian warship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, Libyan officials have said.

    It has been revealed that the strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they mentioned. Several Ukrainian sea drones were rolled out at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, the officials told the Associated Press.

    The officials were affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya.

    There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

    Authorities in divided Libya’s east mentioned in a statement that the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and ⁠resupply on its way back to Russia, ​under maritime cooperation agreements between ‌the two ‌countries.

    Two medical sources told Reuters no deaths had been reported, but there were injuries. The ⁠number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known.

    In a separate attack, another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi on Sunday evening, Libyan military sources told Reuters.

    The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority mentioned port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

    It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible. “The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

    The specialist website Naval News also identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and remarked it was almost certainly destroyed.

    Recent findings suggest that HI Sutton, a naval analyst, mentioned the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”.

    If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

    But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.

    A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

    Initial reports and footage suggest the Merkury was struck from above, potentially by a drone, rolled out no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.

    Sources indicate that russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port, which has a growing importance since it lost bases in Syria, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean.

    Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

    The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

    On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities mentioned.

    The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces stated, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

    Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

    The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

    Finland’s military mentioned last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

    Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

    Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.

    Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.

    All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.

    In a recent development, the challenges with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights. According to The New York Times:.

    The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.

    “Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.
